title: Queen against rook and pawn: the fortresses
summary: With an extra pawn, the rook sometimes draws against the queen. Which pawns hold, how to defend, and how the queen wins when there is no fortress.
practice: Now the practical challenge, with or without a clock. It's Müller and Lamprecht's fortress, and you defend: rook between e3 and g3, king beside the pawn, and don't touch the pawn.
step.buildDone: The fortress is built: pawn on g5, rook on f6 protected by it, king beside them. It's the idea of the previous part, with the knight pawn on the fifth: if the black king comes up against the rook, it waits far away on the f-file and comes back later.
step.beyondWhy: 1.Kg2! With the black king behind our line, queen and king can build a mate together: the side with the queen checks and brings the king up for the mating threat. The defender moves their own king away from the enemy king, without leaving the pawn, and keeps the rook on e3. 1.Kg1 also holds; 1.Rg3 gets away with it here, but in the next position it loses.
part.fortress.title: The second-rank fortress
part.fortress.summary: Rook on a square the pawn protects, king beside it: the queen has nothing to do.
step.t_fortress: Queen against rook and pawn. You have the rook and the pawn, and the queen looks far stronger. White to move. Before I explain, think: is there a way for White never to lose anything?
step.t_fortress.hint1: The f2 pawn protects two squares on the third rank. Find them, and see what happens if the queen takes the rook on one of them.
step.t_fortress.hint2: The rook only needs to go back and forth between those two squares, and the king stays glued to the pawn. The pawn never moves.
step.why: This is the fortress. The rook on e3 is protected by the pawn: if the queen takes it, the f-pawn takes back and only the kings are left. The third rank belongs to the rook, so the black king can't cross it. And our king has g1, h1 and h2 to escape the checks, always beside the pawn. The rook shuttles between e3 and g3, the squares the pawn protects; h3 also works, as long as our king is next to it to protect it.
step.d_shuttle: Watch the rook go back and forth. I play both sides; notice that nothing changes, however hard the queen tries.
step.d_shuttle.m1: 1.Rg3. The rook goes to the other square the pawn protects: a waiting move.
step.d_shuttle.m2: 1...Ke4. The black king wants to come down to d3, behind our line.
step.d_shuttle.m3: 2.Re3+! The rook returns with check. The third rank is the rook's, and the king can't cross it.
step.d_shuttle.m4: 2...Kf4. The king goes back to f4. Taking doesn't help: 2...Qxe3 3.fxe3 Kxe3 leaves only the kings.
step.d_shuttle.m5: 3.Rh3. The third square: the pawn doesn't protect h3, but the king on g2 does.
step.d_shuttle.m6: 3...Qc6+. Check on the long diagonal, which runs through g2.
step.d_shuttle.m7: 4.Kg1. The king steps out of check and stays beside the pawn. The rook on h3 is unprotected for one move, but neither the queen nor the black king can reach it.
step.d_shuttle.m9: 5.Kg2. The king comes back and protects the pawn and the rook again. Two checks, and nothing has changed.
step.shuttle: Now you defend. This fortress came up in Van der Poel against Smits, 2000; here the colours are swapped, the pawn is a centre pawn and the queen has just checked on d4. Block the check with the rook, answer the next check with the king beside the pawn and, when the black king reaches f4, switch the rook to another square.
step.shuttle.hint: The rook has two good squares, d3 and f3. The king has two, d1 and d2, behind the rook.
step.shuttle.done: 1.Rd3 Qb4+ 2.Kd1 Kf4 3.Rf3+ (3.Rh3 also holds): the rook has switched protected squares, always on the third rank. The king stays behind the rook and beside the pawn, and the queen can check as long as it likes.
part.knight.title: Knight pawn: the rook waits far away
part.knight.summary: The knight pawn holds even on the fifth rank. When the enemy king touches the rook, it steps away along the file and comes back later.
step.t_knight: Now the knight pawn, already on b5. The rook is on c6, protected by it, and our king on b4 protects the pawn. But the black king has come up against the rook. White to move. How do you keep the fortress?
step.t_knight.hint1: The pawn protects a6 and c6, and the black king already touches c6.
step.t_knight.hint2: The rook doesn't need to stay glued to the pawn; it needs to stay on the c-file, out of reach of the king and the queen.
step.knight: This is a training position by Schnabelwolke. The knight pawn holds even on the fourth and fifth rank: on the edge side the queen has no room to attack from behind. The rook lives on a square the pawn protects; when the black king comes up against it, it steps away along the same file, to a square neither the king nor the queen attacks, and comes back when the king leaves. Going to a6 doesn't work: 1.Ra6? Qf4+ 2.Ka5 Kc4, and the black king gets in through the file the rook gave up.
step.d_knight: Watch the rook go back and forth along the c-file.
step.d_knight.m1: 1.Rc2! The rook leaves the king's reach and stays on the c-file: the black king can't cross to the queenside.
step.d_knight.m2: 1...Kd4. The king goes after the rook from below.
step.d_knight.m3: 2.Rc6. With the king away from c6, the rook returns to the square the pawn protects.
step.d_knight.m4: 2...Kd5. The king comes up against it again.
step.d_knight.m5: 3.Rc2. And the rook steps away once more. The queen alone can't open a way for the king.
step.m_knight: Now on the other side: knight pawn on g5, rook on f6 and the black king right up against it. Keep the fortress.
step.m_knight.hint: The same idea: the rook waits on the f-file, away from the king.
step.m_knight.done: 1.Rf2! is the textbook move: the rook stays on the f-file, out of the king's reach, and returns to f6 when it leaves. 1.Rf5+, 1.Rc6, 1.Kh4 and 1.Kh5 also hold.
part.build.title: Building the fortress: the pawn first
part.build.summary: With the knight pawn on the fourth, it advances to create the protected square near the king, and only then does the rook go there.
step.build: 1.g5! On g4 the pawn protected f5 and h5, and the rook can't reach either of them in one move; and 1.Rf6? would fall: 1...Qxf6, because nothing protected the rook. With the pawn on the fifth, f6 becomes a protected square near the king. Then the rook goes there.
step.d_build: Another position, with the rook on d6 and the queen on b1. Watch the fortress being built all the way.
step.d_build.m1: 1.g5! The pawn goes to the fifth: now f6 and h6 are protected squares, and the king is already on one of them.
step.d_build.m2: 1...Kc4. The black king hurries to the centre.
step.d_build.m3: 2.Rf6. The rook takes the other square the pawn protects: pawn, rook and king together, the fortress is built.
step.d_build.m5: 3.Kg7. The king steps out of check and moves next to the rook.
step.d_build.m6: 3...Kd5. The black king heads for e6, to come up against the rook.
step.d_build.m7: 4.Kg6. The king returns beside the pawn: it protects g5 and f6 at the same time.
step.m_build: Now you build the fortress: pawn on g4, rook on e6, king on h6. Only one move holds; then take the rook to the square the pawn protects.
step.m_build.hint: Before the rook, the pawn: it has to protect a square near the king.
step.m_build.done: 1.g5! and, after 1...Kd4, 2.Rf6. With the pawn still on g4, 1.Rf6? would lose the rook: 1...Qxf6, because nothing protected it. The pawn creates the protected square, the rook takes it, the king stays beside them.
part.rookPawn.title: Rook pawn on the second: the zugzwang
part.rookPawn.summary: Now with the queen. The rook has a single protected square, and a quiet queen move leaves Black without a good move; then the king comes in too.
step.t_rookPawn: Now you have the queen, in a training position by KaushalK. Rook pawn on h7 and rook on g6, the only square the pawn protects. White to play and win. Find the move that leaves Black without a good move.
step.t_rookPawn.hint1: Don't check. Think of a waiting move that leaves Black without a single good move.
step.t_rookPawn.hint2: The right square does two things at once: it watches the eighth rank and keeps the rook from leaving g6.
step.rookPawnWhy: 1.Qe7, and it's zugzwang. The rook has only one protected square, g6: if 1...Rg7, 2.Qe8 is mate; if it leaves along the sixth or down the g-file, it is unprotected and falls to the ladder of checks you saw in queen against rook, up to the check that hits king and rook together. The king only has h8, and there it is even worse off; and if the pawn moves, the rook loses its defender. With a rook pawn on the second rank the rook needed two squares and has only one.
step.d_zugzwang: Watch the zugzwang at work. The rook leaves, the queen checks, and the position comes back the same, with Black to move again.
step.d_zugzwang.m1: 1.Qe7. No check: the queen watches e8 and f8 and ties the rook to g6.
step.d_zugzwang.m2: 1...Ra6. The rook runs far away; now it has no defender.
step.d_zugzwang.m3: 2.Qd8+. Check along the eighth. The king only has f7 and g7.
step.d_zugzwang.m4: 2...Kg7. The king leaves the eighth, but stays far from the rook on a6.
step.d_zugzwang.m5: 3.Qd7+. Check along the seventh: the most stubborn defence takes the king to the h-file.
step.d_zugzwang.m6: 3...Kh6. On h6 the king stands in front of its own pawn.
step.d_zugzwang.m7: 4.Qc7! The queen waits, watching the seventh: the king cannot go back to g7.
step.d_zugzwang.m8: 4...Rg6. The rook returns to g6, the square the pawn protects.
step.d_zugzwang.m9: 5.Qe7. The same zugzwang, with the black king worse off on h6, and Black to move. Each cycle makes their position worse until the rook falls.
step.d_kingIn: Now the rook's other way out. Watch our king.
step.d_kingIn.m1: 1.Qe7. The zugzwang again: any Black move makes things worse.
step.d_kingIn.m2: 1...Rh6. The rook leaves g6 for the h-file, where the pawn doesn't protect it.
step.d_kingIn.m3: 2.Kg5! Instead of a check, the king comes in: it attacks the rook and gets close to the black king. From here on the king helps to mate too.
step.m_rookPawn: Now on the other side of the board: pawn on a7, rook on b6. Find the move that leaves Black without a good move.
step.m_rookPawn.hint: No check: the queen watches the eighth rank and ties the rook to the square the pawn protects.
step.m_rookPawn.done: 1.Qd7! Zugzwang: the rook cannot leave b6 without losing its protection, and any king move makes things worse.
part.king.title: Carlsen–Matlakov: the king, not the check
part.king.summary: Against a bishop pawn on the third there is no fortress, but the queen alone can't win: the zugzwang and the king that comes behind the pawn.
step.t_king: Carlsen against Matlakov, Grand Swiss on the Isle of Man, 2019. Bishop pawn on the third, rook on d5, and the black king has left the pawn for c4. Carlsen's king is still far away, on g4. White plays the 66th move. Find the move that leaves Black without a waiting move.
step.t_king.hint1: The rook has to stay on the d-file to cut our king off. Which black piece is undefended?
step.t_king.hint2: The queen needs to attack the pawn and, with the same move, take away the squares from which the black king would defend it.
step.kingWhy: How they got here: with 53.Qxg6 Carlsen took Black's bishop and was left with queen against rook and a bishop pawn on the third. There is no fortress, but the queen alone can't win: every check gives the defender time to tidy up the pieces. So Carlsen brought the king, 55.Kg3, 56.Kf4, 59.Ke4, and later manoeuvred to g4. Now 66.Qb6! leaves Black without a good move: the queen attacks c6 and takes b5, c5 and d4 away from the black king.
step.d_walk: The moves of the game from here.
step.d_walk.m1: 66.Qb6! The zugzwang: the queen attacks c6 and takes b5, c5 and d4 away from the black king.
step.d_walk.m3: 67.Kf5! The king doesn't retreat: it advances, heading for e6.
step.d_walk.m4: 67...c5. The pawn leaves c6, where the queen was attacking it.
step.d_walk.m5: 68.Qa5. The queen attacks c5 again and ties the black king to the pawn.
step.d_walk.m6: 68...Rd5+. One more check, which only pushes the white king forward.
step.d_walk.m7: 69.Ke6. The king reaches e6: from there it eyes d6, behind the pawn.
step.d_walk.m8: 69...Rd4. The rook goes back to cutting the king off along the d-file.
step.m_kd6: Nine moves on: after 77...Kd4, the white king is on e6 and the queen on c2. Play Carlsen's 78th move.
step.m_kd6.hint: A check gives Black time back. Which piece hasn't arrived yet?
step.m_kd6.done: 78.Kd6! The king gets behind the pawn. There followed 78...c4 79.Qf2+ Re3 80.Qd2+, and Matlakov resigned: with the white king behind the pawn, the defence had no squares left. It does not always go this way: in 1997 Vaganian, against Bologan, preferred checks in a similar ending and let the win slip twice.
part.beyond.title: When the attacking king crosses the line
part.beyond.summary: The second-rank fortress only exists while the attacking king is on the far side of the third rank. If it has crossed, the defender moves their own king away.
step.d_beyond.m1: 1.Kg2! The king goes far from the black king, still beside the pawn.
step.d_beyond.m3: 2.Kg1. 2.Kf1? would lose: close to the black king, queen and king build the mate.
step.d_beyond.m4: 2...Kc2. The black king comes closer along the second rank.
step.d_beyond.m5: 3.Kh2. Our king goes even further away, and the rook stays on e3, protected by the pawn.
step.m_beyond: The black king is on c2, also behind our line. White to move and hold.
step.m_beyond.hint: Move your king away from the black king, without leaving the pawn.
step.m_beyond.done: 1.Kg2, the demonstration's route: the king far from the black king and the rook on e3. 1.Kg1 and 1.Re2+ also hold. 1.Rg3? would lose: after 1...Qh1+, either our king goes to e2, close to the black king, or the rook gives up the third rank with 2.Rg1.
part.seventh.title: Pawn on the seventh: promote with check and skewer
part.seventh.summary: With the pawn on the seventh, sometimes the draw comes from trading everything: promoting with check and winning the queen back with a rook check.
step.d_seventh: 1.c8=Q+! promotes with check along the file, and the black queen has to take; 1.c8=R+ also holds, and even 1.c8=B. Then comes a rook skewer. Watch everything get traded.
step.d_seventh.m1: 1.c8=Q+! The promotion comes with check along the c-file.
step.d_seventh.m2: 1...Qxc8. Forced: running with the king would leave White with queen and rook.
step.d_seventh.m3: 2.Rc2+! The skewer: the rook attacks the king and, behind it on the same file, the queen.
step.d_seventh.m4: 2...Kd7. The king gets out of check and protects the queen; 2...Kb7 would be the same.
step.d_seventh.m5: 3.Rxc8. The rook takes the queen anyway.
step.d_seventh.m6: 3...Kxc8. Only the kings are left on the board: a draw.
step.m_seventh: Now on the other side: pawn on f7, the black king on f6 attacking it, and the rook on h2. White to move and draw.
step.m_seventh.hint: Promote with check; then look for the king and the queen on the same file.
step.m_seventh.done: Promoting with check forces 1...Qxf8, and 2.Rf2+ skewers king and queen along the f-file: the rook takes the queen, and trading everything is the draw.
part.desperado.title: Pawn on the seventh: the desperado rook
part.desperado.summary: With our king stalemated in the corner, the rook checks without stopping; if it is taken, it is stalemate.
step.t_desperado: Our king is stuck on a8, in front of its own pawn, and Black threatens mate. White to move. Only one move holds. Which?
step.t_desperado.hint1: Our king has no move: if the rook disappears from the board, it is stalemate.
step.t_desperado.hint2: The rook has to check from a square where the queen can't take it, and far from the black king.
step.desperado: 1.Rh6+! It's the desperado rook: it gives check after check, and taking it is stalemate. The check has to come from far away and along a line the queen doesn't cover. 1.Rc1+? loses: 1...Qxc1, and now our king has b8, so there is no stalemate: 2.Kb8 Qb2+, and mate comes next move.
step.d_desperado: Another position with our king stuck in the corner. Watch the desperado rook to the end.
step.d_desperado.m2: 1...Ke4. The black king approaches the rook to stop the checks.
step.d_desperado.m3: 2.Rh4+. The rook drops back and checks again.
step.d_desperado.m5: 3.Rh3+. One more check: the queen cannot reach the rook, and the black king is not attacking it yet.
step.d_desperado.m6: 3...Kg2. The king attacks the rook, thinking the checks are over.
step.d_desperado.m7: 4.Rh2+! The rook offers itself: if the king declines, it keeps checking along the h-file.
step.d_desperado.m8: 4...Kxh2. Stalemate: our king has no move, and it's a draw.
step.m_desperado: Back to the first position: after 1.Rh6+ Kb5, the rook keeps working. Only one move holds.
step.m_desperado.hint: Check again, from a square that neither the queen nor the black king can reach.
step.m_desperado.done: 2.Rh5+ Kb6 3.Rh6+: the desperado rook keeps checking. If the king takes it, it is stalemate; if it runs, another check comes.
part.recap.title: Grigoriev's zugzwang and the summary
part.recap.summary: With the pawn on the sixth and the rook behind it, whoever has the move loses. Then three rules and the defence in the practical challenge.
step.summaryRules: To take with you. One, the fortress: rook on a square protected by the pawn, or by the king, king beside it and the pawn standing still; the knight pawn can go as far as the fifth, and the rook waits far away on its file when the enemy king comes up against it. Two, with the queen: the zugzwang, the check that also hits the loose rook and, against a bishop or centre pawn, the king that comes behind the pawn: the king, not the check. Three, with the pawn on the seventh, the tricks: promoting with check and the skewer, and the desperado rook with the king stalemated. As for the pawns: the knight pawn almost always holds; the rook pawn, on the third, with the king in the corner; the bishop or centre pawn, only on the second.
step.sixth: 1.Kc3! This is Grigoriev's position with Black to move: a draw, the queen has no way to improve. With White to move, White would lose: any move spoils it. It's a reciprocal zugzwang, which is why the king must reach c3 at the right moment, leaving the move to Black.
step.grig: Now on the other side: pawn on d6, rook on d3, our king on g3, in check from the black queen on e1. White to move. Take the king to Grigoriev's square and answer the check without abandoning the rook.
step.grig.hint: The same square, mirrored: on the third rank, without touching the rook.
step.grig.done: 1.Kf3! and, after 1...Qh1+, 2.Ke2 (2.Kf2 and 2.Ke3 also hold), close to the rook. Once the queen leaves the diagonal, the king returns to f3.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: hold the draw. Rook between e3 and g3, king glued to the pawn, and the pawn stays where it is.
key.fortress: The fortress: the rook sits on a square protected by the pawn, with the king next to it. The queen finds no way in, and it is a draw.
key.vdp: Van der Poel vs Smits, 2000: the same fortress with a central pawn. The rook shuttles from one side of the pawn to the other, always protected, and the king just waits.
key.a3: A rook pawn on the third rank still holds: the king hides in the corner and the rook stays glued to it. Any other route loses.
key.c3: A bishop pawn on the third rank makes no fortress: the black king walks round and gets behind the pawn.
key.b5: A knight pawn on the fifth rank still draws: the pawn protects the rook, and on the edge side the queen has no room to attack. When the enemy king comes up against the rook, it waits far away on the same file.
key.rook2: A rook pawn on the second rank makes no fortress: the rook has only one protected square, and a quiet queen move leaves Black with nothing good to play.
key.carlsen: Carlsen vs Matlakov, Grand Swiss on the Isle of Man, 2019: a bishop pawn on the third rank makes no fortress. A quiet queen move left Black with nothing good to play, the white king got behind the pawn, and Matlakov resigned on move 80.
history: With no pawns, the queen always beats the rook. Add a single pawn next to the rook and everything changes: in some positions king, rook and pawn form a fortress, a wall the queen simply cannot break through. The hard part is knowing which positions hold and which fall, and even strong players get it wrong: in 1959 Whitaker announced a draw in a position his opponent was winning. Nikolai Grigoriev published in 1933 a fortress with the pawn on the sixth rank where everything depends on whose move it is, and Karsten Müller and Frank Lamprecht gathered the practical rules in their book Fundamental Chess Endings, in 2001. In 2019, on the Isle of Man, Magnus Carlsen showed Maxim Matlakov how to bring down a fortress that only looks like one: twenty-seven moves of patience, the king walking round until it stood behind the pawn, until Matlakov resigned.
step.t_build: Knight pawn on g4, rook on e6, king on h6, and the black queen on c3. There is no fortress yet. White to move. What is the right order to build it?
step.t_build.hint1: The rook needs a square protected by the pawn. Which squares does the pawn protect now, and can the rook reach any of them?
step.t_build.hint2: Look at the queen's diagonal: if the rook went to f6 now, what would protect it?
step.t_beyond: The second-rank fortress has four conditions: pawn on the second rank, from b to g; rook on the third, protected by the pawn; king beside the pawn; and the attacking king on the far side of the third rank. Here the last one fails: the black king is on b2, behind our line. White to move. How do you hold?
step.t_beyond.hint1: With the black king behind the line, queen and king can build a mate together. Which king is in that danger?
step.t_beyond.hint2: The rook is already fine on e3. Which piece needs to get away from the black king?
step.t_seventh: Pawn on c7, one step from promoting, but the black queen watches c8, and the black king attacks the pawn: if White dawdles, 1...Kxc7, and queen against rook is a loss. White to move and draw. How?
step.t_seventh.hint1: Promoting isn't ruled out just because the queen can take. Look at what is left on the c-file after the capture.
step.t_seventh.hint2: After the capture, the rook has a check that hits two black pieces on the same file.
step.t_grig: A different fortress, by Grigoriev, 1933: pawn on the sixth, rook behind it on e3. Our king is on b3 and the black queen has just given check from d1. White to move. Only one king square holds. Which?
step.t_grig.hint1: Here the move matters: whoever has to play in the key position loses. Look for the square that hands the move to Black.
step.t_grig.hint2: The square is on the third rank, without touching the rook.
step.d_grig: Watch the queen try and the king return to c3.
step.d_grig.m2: 2.Kd2. The king steps out of check towards the rook; 2.Kc2 and 2.Kd3 also hold.
step.d_grig.m3: 2...Qa2+. Another check, now along the second rank.
step.d_grig.m4: 3.Kc3. The king is back on c3, and it is Black to move again: the same zugzwang, and the fortress still stands.
step.seventhRule: The rule: with the pawn on the seventh and the enemy queen watching the promotion square, look to promote with check and then for the rook check that catches king and queen on the same line. Here the rook takes the queen, and only the kings are left.
key.grigoriev: Grigoriev, 1933: pawn on the sixth rank with the rook behind it. Here the move decides everything: if the queen is to play it is a draw; if the rook side had to move, it would lose.
ex.e01: The second-rank fortress, but Black has an extra pawn on h4. Hold the draw.
ex.e01.hint: The extra pawn takes away one of the rook's squares. Which one? And which one is left?
ex.e01.solution: 1.Rh3 (1.Rf3+, 1.Kg1, 1.Kh2 and 1.Kh3 also hold). 1.Rg3 no longer works: 1...hxg3 and the fortress is over. With the black pawn on h4 the rook only has e3 and h3, and the draw still stands.
ex.e02: Knight pawn on the fourth, rook on c4, unprotected. Find the move that keeps the fortress.
ex.e02.hint: The b4 pawn protects a5 and c5. The rook needs one of those squares.
ex.e02.solution: 1.Rc5. The rook goes to the square the pawn protects, beside the king. 1.Kc3 also holds, but leaves the rook on c4 for the queen to attack. A knight pawn on the fourth is still a fortress.
ex.e03: Marcotulli against Malström, 2001, with colours reversed. Bring the pieces to the knight-pawn fortress.
ex.e03.hint: Knight pawn on the fifth, rook on a square it protects, king beside the pawn.
ex.e03.solution: 1.b5, 2.Rc6 and 3.Ka6 is the simple way: the pawn on the fifth, the rook on a square it protects and the king close by. Rook moves along the c-file also hold, because the pawn can advance later. In the game, the defender gave a rook check at the wrong moment and lost.
ex.e04: Knight pawn on the fourth, rook on c5 protected by the pawn, but the black king is right next to it. Which move holds?
ex.e04.hint: The rook can wait on the c-file, but not within the black king's reach.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Rc8 (1.Rc7, 1.Rc6, 1.Rc1 and 1.Kb6 also hold). The rook waits on the c-file, away from the black king; after the queen's waiting move it returns to c5. 1.Rc3 loses at once to 1...Kxc3, and 1.Rc2 and 1.Rc4 lose as well.
ex.e05: A training position: rook pawn on the second, the rook on g6 and the black king in the corner. Force the rook in front of the king and close in with your king.
ex.e05.hint: Two checks force the rook in front of the king, and then our king steps in.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Qf8+, 1...Rg8 forced; 2.Qf6+, 2...Rg7 forced; and 3.Kh6. The rook is pinned in front of the king and the mate on g7 can't be stopped.
ex.e06: Whitaker against Ferriz, 1959, with colours reversed. The rook on e6 is not protected by the pawn. Only one move wins.
ex.e06.hint: A check on the diagonal that reaches h7. Then another attack on the rook, with or without check.
ex.e06.solution: 1.Qc2+. If 1...Kg8, 2.Qc8+ and 3.Qxe6. If 1...Kh6, 2.h5 (2.Qd3 and king moves such as 2.Kg4 also win): the pawn takes g6 from the black king, 2...Kxh5 runs into mate in a few moves, and with no squares for the king the rook falls in the end. In the game, the side with the rook announced a draw in a lost position.
ex.e07: Vaganian against Bologan, 1997. Queen against rook and a bishop pawn on the fourth. Only one move wins.
ex.e07.hint: Checks hand the fortress back to the defender. Bring the king closer.
ex.e07.solution: 95.Kf4, the only move: the king heads for e3 and d3, behind the pawn. In the game Vaganian checked, let the fortress come back twice, and only won because Bologan made the last mistake.
ex.e08: The second-rank fortress is set up, but our king is already past the sixth rank. Only one move wins.
ex.e08.hint: With the king this close, the threat is mate. Start with a check along the eighth and bring the king to g7.
ex.e08.solution: 1.Qb8+, 1...Ke7 (the only move) and 2.Kg7, threatening mate on f8. The rook has to leave, and the queen takes d8: the black king is stuck in front of its pawn and the pawn falls. With Black to move, 1...Kc7 or 1...Kc8 would draw.
ex.e09: A study by Pogosyants: rook and pawn on the seventh against the queen, with the black king in front of the pawn. Find the draw.
ex.e09.hint: Check first, to drive the black king off c8. Then our king steps out of the pin, and the pawn promotes with check.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Rc2+, 1...Kd8; 2.Kb8, so the pawn is no longer pinned; the queen goes to f5 and 3.f8=Q+ forces the trade; then 4.Rc8+ and the rook takes the queen. 2.Rf2 on the second move also draws.
ex.e10: A study by Prokeš: pawn on c7, rook on c8 and the black queen ready to check. Six moves, nearly all of them the only move. Find the draw.
ex.e10.hint: The rook goes to the one square from which, after the pawn is lost, it can still check all the way to stalemate.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Rd8, then after the checks 2.Kb7 and 3.Ka8; when the queen takes on c7, 4.Rd5+, 5.Rb5+ and 6.Rb6+: the black king has to take the rook and stalemates ours. Any other rook square on the first move loses the pawn without the trick.
